title: Sensex Crashes 2,700 Points in Two Days as Oil Spike Rattles Dalal Street
excerpt: India benchmark indices suffer their steepest two-day fall in months as Brent crude tops $107 and the rupee plumbs record lows
body:
Indian equity markets endured a bruising two-day selloff that wiped out over ₹12 lakh crore in investor wealth, as a toxic cocktail of surging crude oil prices, a collapsing rupee, and heavy foreign selling sent the Sensex tumbling 2,769 points across May 11-12.

**The Rout in Numbers:** The BSE Sensex closed at 74,559.24 on May 12, down 1,456 points in a single session after already shedding 1,313 points the previous day. The NSE Nifty 50 settled at 23,379.55, breaching a key psychological support level. Market breadth was overwhelmingly negative, with declining stocks outnumbering advancers nearly four to one on both exchanges.

**Why Markets Crumbled:** The immediate trigger was Brent crude surging past $107 a barrel after Donald Trump dismissed Irans latest ceasefire proposal, dashing hopes of a swift resolution to the US-Iran conflict. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, making it acutely vulnerable to sustained price spikes. The Indian rupee compounded the pain, hitting a record low of 95.63 against the dollar on May 12, raising the effective cost of oil imports even further.

Foreign institutional investors were aggressive net sellers, pulling out an estimated 4,200 crore rupees across both sessions. IT heavyweights Infosys and TCS led sectoral declines after OpenAI announced an enterprise AI deployment venture that spooked investors about competitive pressures on Indian outsourcers.

**The Macro Squeeze:** Prime Minister Narendra Modis unusual public appeal for austerity, urging citizens to work from home, cut fuel consumption, and reduce gold purchases, amplified anxiety rather than calming it. Opposition leaders seized on the remarks as evidence of a looming economic crisis.

The Reserve Bank of India has been intervening in currency markets to slow the rupees decline, but forex reserves have fallen to their lowest level in over a year, limiting the central banks firepower. Analysts warn that if oil sustains above $100 through Q2, Indias current account deficit could widen to 3.2 percent of GDP, a level not seen since 2013.

**The NRI Portfolio Hit:** For the 4.4 million Indian-Americans, many of whom hold Indian mutual funds, direct equities, or NRE deposits, the double blow of a falling Sensex and weakening rupee translates into compounded dollar-denominated losses. An NRI who invested $100,000 in a Nifty index fund at the start of 2026 has now lost roughly 14 percent in dollar terms, split between market decline and currency erosion.

**What to Watch:** All eyes turn to Indias April CPI inflation data due this week, which could show the first breach above the RBIs 6 percent upper band in over a year. If oil stays elevated and the rupee continues sliding, an emergency rate decision or fresh forex intervention measures cannot be ruled out.
nri_angle: NRIs with Indian market exposure face compounded losses from both the Sensex decline and rupee weakness, eroding dollar-denominated returns on mutual funds, equities, and NRE deposits by roughly 14 percent year-to-date.
author: Diaspora Desk
